answer: Regression to the mean is the statistical tendency for extreme measurements to move closer to the average on remeasurement, which creates the illusion that an intervention targeting extreme cases worked. The tutorial selects the 10 clinics with the highest emergency department visit rates in 2019, averaging 142 visits per 1,000, then a quality improvement program runs and rates fall to 118 by 2021. Yet comparison clinics that received no program fell to 116 over the same period, nearly identical, showing the drop was largely a mathematical certainty of selecting on extreme baseline values.

faqs.q: Why do the worst-performing units improve even without an intervention?
faqs.a: Any measurement combines true performance and random variation, so units selected for extreme values were partly there by chance and tend to move toward the average on remeasurement. The tutorial's untreated comparison clinics improved about as much as the program clinics.

faqs.q: How does targeting extreme baseline values create a false program effect?
faqs.a: Selecting the most extreme cases guarantees they will likely improve on their own, so the apparent gain reflects regression to the mean rather than the program. The tutorial calls this a mathematical certainty, not evidence of effectiveness.

faqs.q: What designs handle regression to the mean?
faqs.a: The tutorial describes three approaches, including using a comparison group of equally extreme but untreated units, so that the program effect is measured against the natural regression those units would also show.
